lessons.title: How Scientific Investigations Work
lessons.reading: Scientists study the natural world by asking questions and collecting evidence. A hypothesis is a possible explanation that can be investigated. In a fair experiment, researchers change one variable while trying to keep other conditions consistent. They record observations, compare results, and consider possible sources of error. A strong conclusion describes what the evidence supports and what remains uncertain. For example, a student could compare plant growth under different lighting conditions while keeping water and soil similar. Repeated measurements can help determine whether the observed changes are consistent.

flashcards.back: A condition kept similar between groups in a fair investigation.
Observations or measurements supporting a conclusion.

lessons.title: Living Cells and Energy
objectives: Describe cells as building blocks of life
lessons.reading: Living organisms are made of cells. Some organisms consist of a single cell, while others contain many specialized cells working together. Cells use energy to grow, repair structures, transport materials, and carry out everyday processes. In many plants, chloroplasts use light to help produce sugars during photosynthesis. Animal and plant cells both have structures that carry out important tasks. Scientists use microscopes to examine small cell structures. When comparing different kinds of cells, students should note similarities, differences, and the limitations of the equipment they are using.

flashcards.back: The basic structural and functional unit of living organisms.
The process by which plants and certain other organisms use light to make sugars.
